meaning: The part of a machine a job exhausts first, while the other parts sit partly idle.
The hardware counters inside a processor core, each of which counts one kind of event such as a clock cycle or a retired micro-operation.

One page of readings for one workload on one machine: throughput, where the CPU's slots went, what lies behind the largest loss, the GPU readings where a GPU does the work, and how it was all counted.
The Linux tool that reads the processor's counters; perf stat runs a program and prints the totals.

What perf does when it cannot count every requested event at once: the events take turns, each count is scaled to the whole run, and perf reports the share of the measurement time each counter was running.
One of the smaller internal steps a core splits each program instruction into; Intel writes uOp.
Finished instructions divided by clock cycles: how much a core got done per cycle, with nothing on why the rest of its capacity went unused.
The part of a core that predicts the next instructions, fetches them and decodes them into micro-operations.
The part of a core that executes micro-operations in its arithmetic and memory units, out of program order where that is faster.
The last pipeline stage, where the results of executed micro-operations are made final in program order.
The stage that divides a core's front end from its back end; Arm counts slots there.
Fetching and running instructions after a branch before knowing which way the branch goes, on a guess.
Throwing away the micro-operations started after a wrong branch guess and restarting from the right place.
One chance, in one clock cycle, to pass one micro-operation from the front end to the back end; a core has a fixed number per cycle.
A core's slots per cycle, for example 10 on the Cortex-X925 and Neoverse V3 and 5 on the Cortex-A725.
A method, from a 2014 Intel paper, that sorts every slot of every cycle into one of four buckets to show where a core's capacity went.
The share of slots that carried a micro-operation which finished and was kept: the useful work.
The share of slots that carried work thrown away after a wrong branch guess, plus, in the corrected formulas, slots lost while recovering from it.
The share of slots left empty because the front end had no micro-operation ready.
The share of slots left empty because the back end could not accept another micro-operation.

The part of back-end bound in which the core is waiting for data to be loaded or stored; faster memory helps it: more bandwidth if the loads stream, lower latency if each load waits for the one before.
The part of back-end bound in which execution units are busy or operations wait on each other's results; a faster core helps it, and faster memory does not.
A separate counter's share of cycles in which the back end waited on memory.
Arm events counting micro-operations dispatched through a slot (including those later thrown away) and micro-operations that retired.
The Arm event counting empty slots; it is the sum of STALL_SLOT_FRONTEND and STALL_SLOT_BACKEND.
Arm's per-core adjustment that moves the slots lost while recovering from a flush from front-end bound to bad speculation.
The Arm event that counts cycles the front end spent recovering from a flush, used by the Neoverse V3, Cortex-X925 and Cortex-A725 formulas.
Two hardware threads sharing one processor core; AMD's top-down adds a bucket for slots lost to the other thread.
The Arm processors AWS designs for EC2; Graviton2, 3, 4 and 5 use the Neoverse N1, V1, V2 and V3 cores.
NVIDIA's desktop machine with two Arm core types, the larger Cortex-X925 and the smaller Cortex-A725, and a GB10 GPU.
NVIDIA's small robot computer, with Cortex-A78AE cores; Arm publishes no top-down file for that core.
A physics simulator; the sample card is one core stepping a MuJoCo humanoid model as a stand-in for the arm's simulation.
An EC2 instance with no virtual machine layer between the operating system and the hardware.
One function launched on the GPU, such as a matrix multiply; unrelated to the operating system's kernel.
The GPU's processing unit, repeated many times across the chip.
Units inside each GPU multiprocessor with a pipeline of their own for matrix multiply-accumulate instructions, the arithmetic of training and inference.
The GPU units that find what each camera ray hits when an image is rendered; no counter for them was located in the documentation of nvidia-smi, DCGM, tegrastats or Nsight Compute.
The percent of time in the sample period during which at least one kernel was running on the GPU; it says nothing about how much of the GPU the kernel used.
The Jetson's always-on monitor: GPU activation time, memory-controller bandwidth in use and power per rail.
NVIDIA's fleet monitoring service, which adds SM activity, tensor activity and memory activity per GPU.
The fraction of time at least one group of threads was active on a GPU multiprocessor; threads waiting on memory count as active.
The fraction of cycles the GPU's tensor pipeline was active.
NVIDIA's profiler that puts CPU samples, GPU calls and kernels of one application on a single timeline.
NVIDIA's profiler for one GPU kernel, reporting throughput against the GPU's maximum and a roofline chart.
A chart of a kernel's achieved speed against arithmetic per byte of memory moved, under a roof whose sloped part is the memory bandwidth limit and whose flat part is the peak compute limit.
The second level of top-down analysis, which splits back-end bound into memory bound and core bound; Arm's files for the Neoverse V3, Cortex-X925 and Cortex-A725 define it with events of their own.
The GPU's general floating-point path, as opposed to the tensor pipeline; a kernel whose name carries simt did its arithmetic there.
The PyTorch setting that decides whether a float32 matrix multiply may compute in a lower internal precision; "highest", the default, keeps float32, and "high" permits TensorFloat32.
A number format that stores 10 mantissa bits where float32 stores 23; PyTorch may use it for a float32 matrix multiply when the precision setting is "high".

The section of a kernel profile that reports compute and memory throughput; each figure is the highest of the percentages its constituent counters report, so it need not be a share of the chip's peak arithmetic rate or memory bandwidth.
